request.system: You are a senior clinical coder in an Australian public hospital with fifteen years of experience coding inpatient episodes in ICD-10-AM. You are careful, conservative, and you never invent a code you are not sure of the chapter for.

messages.content:
Code the episode of care below. The principal diagnosis is the single condition established after investigation to be chiefly responsible for the patient's episode of admitted care. It is not the patient's most serious comorbidity, not the presenting symptom, and not the procedure performed. Give the three-character ICD-10-AM category for the principal diagnosis.

Hospital course:
Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: Not provided
Age: 40 years
Gender: Female

Hospital Course:

The patient was admitted to TCVGH due to severe acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) caused by wasp stings. Upon arrival, the patient had respiratory distress and was noted to have nearly 100 painful, reddish, and itchy papules. The initial laboratory examinations showed abnormal liver function tests, high LDH, CK, and increased creatinine level. Additionally, the patient had 3+ dipstick proteinuria and 5 to 10 red blood cells per high power field in urinalysis.

Intravenous corticosteroid and anti-histamine agents were administered, and the patient underwent intubation and protective ventilation with low tidal volume and high positive end-expiratory pressure. The patient also underwent sedation, neuromuscular blockade, hemodialysis, and plasmapheresis. Anuria was observed for nearly 10 days, and the patient received eight sessions of hemodialysis.

The respiratory condition improved gradually, and the patient was extubated on day 8. The levels of CK, AST, ALT, and LDH peaked on day 2 and recovered with the aforementioned management. The patient was discharged on day 24 with creatinine 7.12 mg/dl. During follow-up in the outpatient department, the creatinine returned to normal (Cr:1.16) on day 71.
Diagnosis: [diagnosis section withheld]
Plan:

The patient was discharged with recommendations for follow-up care and monitoring, including regular visits with a nephrologist and an annual physical exam. The patient should avoid future exposure to wasp stings to prevent recurrence of ARDS.

The patient was provided with educational information about wasp stings and the risks associated with this condition. They were advised to seek prompt medical attention in case of any adverse reactions in the future.

Disposition:

Discharged.

Answer in the form CODE: <letter><digit><digit>

text:
The episode centres on a wasp sting causing a systemic toxic reaction, with ARDS, rhabdomyolysis, hepatic injury, acute kidney injury and possible hemolysis. The question is which condition was chiefly responsible for the admission.

In ICD-10-AM, a venom sting is coded to the injury or poisoning chapter. T63.4 (toxic effect of venom of other arthropods) covers wasp venom. Anaphylaxis from a sting would go to T78.2 or T63. This patient had about 100 stings and a toxic reaction rather than a pure allergic one.

Principal diagnosis in the injury chapter is normally the nature of the injury or poisoning. The external cause (X23 contact with hornets, wasps and bees) is not used as the principal diagnosis. The toxic effect of venom, T63, is the condition that explains the ARDS, rhabdomyolysis and AKI. The alternatives are the ARDS (J80) or the acute kidney injury (N17). Coding rules say that when a toxic effect is the cause of the manifestations, the toxic effect (T-code) is sequenced first and the manifestations are coded as additional diagnoses. The mass envenomation is therefore the underlying cause of the whole episode, so T63 is the principal diagnosis.

CODE: T63
